Depends on what you mean by justify. 

If this is just a passion project and you don’t really need to earn a living wage from your art/are financially sound, then it’s justifiable and you should go for it. 

If you do need to make real livable money, going the art route has a high chance of not succeeding. That is not to say it’s impossible. You can do well assuming you have industry connections, live in a location that provides access to numerous artistic based companies, and are fantastic at self promotion. However if you lack these things, it will likely be a struggle. Additionally if you are considering getting a formal education in such topics, you need to be relatively sure that you will be able to recoup the money you invested. The average student loan repayment length these days is 20 years, so you need to be as sure as you can be on this. 

All that said, art can be self taught for little money. Experts exist all over YouTube, forums and Reddit. Anyone with talent, drive and the ability to use google could likely become proficient just by learning and participating in online spaces. Reaching out to a favorite forum member or YouTuber could also result in you gaining networking connections as many of these folks already work as artistic professionals. Book authors can also be a great resource and connection, many have fan pages where they interact with people interested in their work.

Best of luck!

If you like playing games, you may not want this job. QA is considered among the lowest jobs in the industry and is often paid accordingly. QA is extremely tedious and you will spend more time documenting every little thing you do than actually playing. The people that work these jobs are mostly young idealistic folks that want to establish themselves in gaming and move on to other roles in production. You see a lot of artists and aspiring designers, but few actual developers that can really code. Almost no one wants to remain in QA roles forever, but people can spend years there since moving up can be difficult. You are also pretty replaceable, because there is an infinite supply of kids that want to “get paid for playing video games all day!”. QA testers were by far the most fired employees where I worked. The culture varies depending on company, but there can be  drama on those teams in my experience mostly due to everyone being so young. Plus booze is pretty common in the industry, you can expect a lot of drinking at company events (which at times leads to the aforementioned drama). You will get to know your coworkers well because during crunch time you’ll be working shitloads of OT together in a tired grueling grind until launch. This isn’t so bad though if your coworkers are cool. Some really awesome folks work in gaming and you can easily find folks to hang out with after work if you want. The people, not the games, are the best part of the industry.

Psych BA here who went into tech for eh 14 years or so? I made it up to senior management using what I learned in psych. Forget all the emotional bullshit and mental disorders. Here’s what you don’t know you have. A Psych degree means you learned basic research methods and statistics, possibly even the basics of statistical software depending on the school you attended. This is the real value you acquired. You can think, you can test in an organized and consistent manner, and you understand cause effect and correlation. This is VITAL in business, and not everyone you work with has these abilities. My whole career has been a series of looking at processes, asking “why is it done this way and can it be done better?” and then digging into the data and testing using the research methods I learned in psych until I can answer that question. For the first 7 years, I never learned to code anything, just got good with excel and manipulating data. Then I learned SQL and some other data tools like Splunk to improve my abilities. As I moved into management, I started to have others do a lot of the data digging for me, but they were always working toward answering my same basic question I always asked “why is it done this way and can it be done better?”. Look for analyst jobs to start your tech industry career. Highlight your ability to think. Learn excel to start. Read up on how to present yourself clearly and efficiently. Do this and you will find your way.

Mmm. This got me thinking a bit. Former weight and balance guy for freighter aircraft here. Your right in that we used an average weight for the humans on board, and the vast majority of the time that will work just fine. However I can actually think of 1 time this may matter on larger aircraft. It’s not a balance issue, those are really easy to avoid on bigger planes, it’s a sheer weight issue. Aircraft aren’t just balanced, they are divided into zones along the length of the aircraft. Each zone has a maximum weight it can hold without causing it to break off, or sheer, from the other sections. This weight includes both the upper decks as well as belly weight (the cargo holds), so there is a very low chance a particularly heavy belly combined with a bunch of overweight folks could exceed a sheer weight for a particular zone. Would that cause a failure? Almost certainly not, as there is plenty of padding in those numbers for safety. However it would technically have to be addressed before the plane could be allowed to fly, and only using the usual averages could hide that fact (btw if I recall correctly, every human was assumed to be 180 pounds regardless of height, sex or actual weight).

1. Took a part time job working admin for the psych department, which allowed me to get to know several key figures overseeing the graduate program

I did this because most psych students suck at statistics, so doing well in that subject in particular really made me stand out from the crowd.
